Five
FYVE
n., adj.
Old English fīf; Latin quinque (source of “quintet,” “quintessence”); Greek pente (source of “Pentateuch,” “Pentecost”); Hebrew chamesh — all from Proto-Indo-European *penkwe-.

Biblical Definition

Five in Scripture is the number most visibly associated with grace, provision, and the fullness of God’s instructional word. Its most prominent occurrence is the Pentateuch—the five books of Moses, the foundational law-covenant of Israel and the spine of the entire biblical canon. From Genesis through Deuteronomy, the five-book Torah constitutes the complete law of God’s covenant people. The parable of the ten virgins divides evenly: five foolish and five prudent (Matt 25:2), making five the measure of both wisdom and folly before the coming Bridegroom. In the miracle of the loaves, five loaves of bread feed five thousand men through Christ’s blessing (Matt 14:17–19), compressing the pattern of Mosaic manna provision into a new covenant sign. The pool of Bethesda, site of Christ’s healing on the Sabbath, had five colonnades (John 5:2), perhaps evoking the five-book law under which the lame man had waited thirty-eight years without relief. Isaiah prophesied that five cities in Egypt would one day “In that day shall five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the LORD of hosts; one shall be called, The city of destruction.” (Isa 19:18) — a Gentile harvest foreshadowing what the Spirit would accomplish at Pentecost. David chose five smooth stones before Goliath (1 Sam 17:40), though God’s grace needed only one. Five is grace sufficient: not the cosmic fullness of seven, but the abundant provision of a God who teaches and feeds His people.

Webster 1828 Definition

The cardinal number five; in Scripture, the number of the Pentateuch, of grace and provision, associated with the law of God and with the miraculous feeding that points to Christ as the true bread from heaven.

expand to see more

FIVE, adj. & n. One more than four; in Scripture, characteristically the number of the law-covenant (five books of Moses) and of grace extended through provision and teaching. The Pentateuch, the five wise virgins, the five loaves, and the five cities of Isaiah all cluster around this figure.

From Greek pente comes “Pentateuch” (five-scroll Torah) and “Pentecost” (fiftieth day — five times ten), linking the number directly to the fullness of the Mosaic covenant and its Spirit-empowered fulfillment.

Key Scripture

Matthew 25:2 — "And five of them were wise, and five were foolish."

Matthew 14:17 — "And they say unto him, We have here but five loaves, and two fishes."

John 5:2 — "Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches."

Isaiah 19:18 — "In that day shall five cities in the land of Egypt speak the language of Canaan, and swear to the LORD of hosts; one shall be called, The city of destruction."

Modern Corruption

Modern prosperity teaching counts the five-fold ministry (Eph 4:11) as a license for apostolic hierarchy and spiritual authority structures that replace the local church’s eldership with self-styled “apostles”; pop numerology reads five as a “grace number” in abstraction from its Pentateuchal anchor.

expand to see more

The so-called “five-fold ministry” drawn from Ephesians 4:11 has been weaponized by charismatic and New Apostolic Reformation circles to establish permanent offices of apostle and prophet above the local church. This flattens Paul’s listing of gifts given at the ascension into an ecclesiastical polity Scripture does not authorize and the confessions do not recognize.

New Age and metaphysical systems adopt five as the “number of man” (five fingers, five senses, the pentagram) and treat it as a symbol of humanistic completeness. This severs five from its scriptural moorings in law and grace, inverting the biblical meaning: the Pentateuch is not a monument to human achievement but to God’s covenant condescension to instruct and save His people.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the same Indo-European root as “fist” (the five fingers), five acquired its deepest meaning not from counting hands but from the five-book Torah — the hand of God writing His law for His people.

expand to see more

Old English fīf — five; related to fist (five-fingered hand) in Germanic roots.

Latin quinque — five; source of “quintet,” “quintessence,” “quinary.”

Greek pente — five; source of “Pentateuch” (five-scroll law) and “Pentecost” (fiftieth day).

Hebrew chamesh — five; the Pentateuch (chamishsháh chumśhê hatôrâh = the five-fifths of the law).

Proto-Indo-European *penkwe- — five; shared ancestor of all the above.

Usage

"The five wise virgins had oil in their lamps — a readiness that cannot be borrowed at the last hour from those who have prepared by grace."

"Christ’s blessing of five loaves to feed five thousand is not magic but the sign of the true Moses, the greater Prophet who gives the bread of life to all who come."

"The five books of Moses remain the spine of the biblical canon: no New Testament text is rightly read apart from the Pentateuch that frames it."
